---
title: "Input data"
subtitle: "What a run needs, in what form, how to bring your own data, and the alternatives when you have none"
---

A run reads six kinds of **prepared input**. Each is a dataset in a standard form,
stored in `<paths > cache>/inputs/<kind>/<name>/` with a short description,
`input.json`. The experiment file names which dataset of each kind a run uses
(section `inputs`). The source of a dataset does not matter: your own data is
always the first choice, and the global datasets listed under **Alternatives**
fill the gaps where you have none.

| Kind | Required | Used for | Standard form | Made with |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [`weather`](#weather) | yes | every simulated day | daily netCDF per variable and year, regular lat/lon grid | `prepare_weather.py` |
| [`crop_mask`](#crop-mask) | yes | which weather cells are simulated, and the area that weights every result | GeoTIFF of crop hectares per pixel, any grid and CRS | `prepare_crop_mask.py` |
| [`soil`](#soil) | yes | the soil profile of each weather cell | DSSAT `.SOL` file plus `soil_map.csv` | `prepare_soils.py` |
| [`water_regime`](#water-regime) | no | irrigated or rainfed management | GeoTIFF of classes, or of the irrigated share | `prepare_layers.py` |
| [`region`](#region-and-zones) | no | which crop belongs to the area | GeoTIFF of classes | `prepare_layers.py` |
| [`zones`](#region-and-zones) | no | one planting calendar per zone | GeoTIFF of classes | `prepare_layers.py` |

## How preparing works

Every kind follows the same four steps.

1. **Look at your file.** `--inspect` prints what a file holds: variables and
   units, grid and CRS, time steps, the most common values.

   ```bash
   python scripts/prepare_weather.py --inspect <file>
   python scripts/prepare_crop_mask.py --inspect <file>
   python scripts/prepare_layers.py --inspect <file>
   ```

2. **Describe it** in the `prepare` section of the experiment file: where the
   file is, what its values mean, and the name of the dataset to write.
   [`configs/rice-java.yml`](https://github.com/bennyistanto/xdssat/blob/main/configs/rice-java.yml)
   explains every setting;
   [`configs/rice-java-all-options.yml`](https://github.com/bennyistanto/xdssat/blob/main/configs/rice-java-all-options.yml)
   has a complete example of each.

3. **Run the prepare script.** It converts the file to the standard form, writes
   `input.json` and checks the result against the requirements below.

4. **Use it**: set `inputs > <kind>` to the new name. Before every run the same
   checks run again, and a problem stops the run with a message that names the
   setting, what is wrong and how to fix it.

```bash
python scripts/register_inputs.py --list   # the prepared datasets, and whether the experiment's choice passes
```

File paths in the `prepare` section may use the folders of the `paths` section:
`{inputs}`, `{cache}`, `{agera5}`, `{soilgrids}`, `{engine}`. A `*` in a file
name matches several files, for example the tiles of one map.

## Weather

**Used for:** the daily weather of every simulated season. Each weather cell is
one DSSAT weather file.

### Standard form

| Variable | Meaning | Unit | Required |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SRAD` | solar radiation, daily total | MJ m⁻² d⁻¹ | yes |
| `TMAX` | maximum air temperature | °C | yes |
| `TMIN` | minimum air temperature | °C | yes |
| `RAIN` | precipitation, daily total | mm d⁻¹ | yes |
| `DEWP` | dew point temperature | °C | no |
| `WIND` | wind run | km d⁻¹ | no |

- Daily values on a regular latitude-longitude grid of any cell size, at most
  999 rows by 9,999 columns.
- One CF netCDF file per variable and year, stored as integers with a scale of
  0.1 (the weather files reach the engine with one decimal).
- Every run year and the year after it: a season planted late in a year runs
  into the next one.
- The measurement heights of temperature (default 2 m) and wind (10 m for most
  reanalyses, 2 m for NASA POWER) are written into each weather file.

### Bring your own

Section `prepare > weather`, then `python scripts/prepare_weather.py`. Each
variable can come from its own source, for example rain from one product and
temperature from another.

**Gridded daily files** (netCDF). For each variable give `files` (with `{year}`
where the year goes, or `*`) and `variable` (its name in the file). The script:

- cuts each variable to `aoi > bbox` plus one cell (or `box`);
- converts it to DSSAT units from the file's own `units` attribute. Understood:
  K, °C, J m⁻², MJ m⁻², W m⁻², kWh m⁻², metres or kg m⁻² of rain, mm, m s⁻¹,
  km h⁻¹, km d⁻¹. A file without a units attribute needs `units:` per variable;
- takes wind from one speed variable, or from two components `[u, v]`;
- puts every variable on one grid (`grid_step`, or the grid of the TMAX
  source). `regrid` per variable: `exact` (same cells), `mean` (area mean, for a
  finer source), `linear` (bilinear from the cells with data, for a coarser
  source) or `nearest`. Left out, it is chosen from the two grids. Longitudes
  0-360 and either latitude order are handled.

**Sub-daily files** (for example ERA5-Land hourly) need `daily:` per variable,
which says how a day is made:

| `daily:` | For | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `max` | daily maximum of instantaneous values | TMAX from hourly 2 m temperature |
| `min` | daily minimum | TMIN |
| `mean` | daily mean | DEWP, WIND |
| `sum` | amounts per time step | hourly rain totals |
| `accumulated` | running totals since 00 UTC | ERA5-Land precipitation and radiation |

`utc_offset_hours` (for Java, 7) makes the days local. The files of the years
before and after are read too, so the first and last local day of a year are
complete; a missing day stops the preparation with its date.

**Point sources** (weather stations, NASA POWER points) go under `points:`
instead of `variables:`, with `grid_step`. Each point is a DSSAT `.WTH` file or
a CSV table; every cell of the grid takes the series of its nearest point.

- A NASA POWER daily point download (CSV) is read as it is: the location, the
  parameter names (`T2M_MAX`, `T2M_MIN`, `PRECTOTCORR`, `ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN`,
  `T2MDEW`, `WS2M`) and their units come from its header; -999 is no data.
- Your own table needs a date column (`DATE`, or `YEAR` with `DOY`, or `YEAR`,
  `MO`, `DY`), `columns:` (which column holds which variable), `units:` and the
  location (`lat`, `lon`) if the file does not give it.
- Every point needs SRAD, TMAX, TMIN and RAIN on every day of the years; a gap
  stops the preparation with the date.

### Alternatives

| Dataset | Grid | Period | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| [AgERA5](https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.6c68c9bb) | 0.1°, daily | 1979 to present | all six variables; agrometeorological indicators derived from ERA5; CC BY 4.0 (Climate Data Store record) |
| [ERA5-Land](https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.e2161bac) | 0.1°, hourly | 1950 to present | use `daily:` per variable; precipitation and radiation are accumulated since 00 UTC; CC BY 4.0 (Climate Data Store record) |
| [W5E5 v2.0](https://doi.org/10.48364/ISIMIP.342217) | 0.5°, daily | 1979 to 2019 | WFDE5 over land merged with ERA5 over the ocean, the ISIMIP3 reference climate; all six variables; CC0 (DataCite record) |
| [MSWEP v2.8](https://www.gloh2o.org/mswep/) | 0.1°, 3-hourly | 1979 to present | rain only, merged gauge, satellite and reanalysis; CC BY-NC 4.0 (stated by the [ICDC Hamburg mirror](https://www.cen.uni-hamburg.de/en/icdc/data/atmosphere/mswep-precipitation-amount.html), not checked at GloH2O); use `daily: sum` |
| [NASA POWER](https://power.larc.nasa.gov/docs/services/api/temporal/daily/) | point or region | see the POWER documentation | daily; meteorology from MERRA-2 (0.5° x 0.625°), radiation from CERES; free download per point (CSV) |
| [CHIRPS 3.0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-026-07096-4) | 0.05°, daily | 1981 to present | rain only, 60°S-60°N; combine with temperature and radiation from another source |

### What the checks refuse

A missing required variable; a year without files; a grid that is not regular
or has more than 999 x 9,999 cells; for gridded sources, a unit that is not
understood; for points, a day without data.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Tested on Java

- Java weather prepared from the global AgERA5 archive (2015-2017, all six
  variables) is identical value by value to the AgERA5 cache of the case study
  (2.1 million values per variable), and a full Java run with it gives the same
  results for all 5,658 seasons of 2015-2016.
- The same weather at 0.25°: 227 cells instead of 1,187, the same total rice
  area, area-weighted yields within 2% of the 0.1° run.
- A NASA POWER point download for Bandung (2015-2016) is read without settings;
  a 2015 run of 20 cells on it ran all 51 seasons.
- Hourly files and station tables are tested with synthetic files
  (`tests/test_weather_sources.py`).
:::

## Crop mask

**Used for:** which weather cells are simulated, and the hectares that weight
every result. The soil profile of a cell is also weighted by the crop under it.

### Standard form

- A GeoTIFF on any north-up grid and CRS (degrees, UTM, equal-area ...).
- Band 1: crop area per pixel; `units_per_ha` in `input.json` says how many
  units make a hectare (1 for hectares; 100 for the percent of a 1 ha pixel).
- Optional second band with a crop class (for example the field type); it is
  kept as a column of the strata.
- Each pixel goes to the weather cell under it. A pixel coarser than about
  100 m is read as sub-points about 100 m apart (at most 10 x 10 per pixel),
  each with its part of the area, so it is shared between the weather cells and
  the water regime, region and soil classes it covers.

### Bring your own

Section `prepare > crop_mask`, then `python scripts/prepare_crop_mask.py`.
`values:` says what the map holds:

| `values:` | Map | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| `classes` | a land-cover or crop-type map | `classes:` the codes of the crop |
| `fraction`, `percent` | the crop's share of each pixel | |
| `ha`, `m2`, `km2` | crop area per pixel | |
| `polygons` | a vector file of fields | optional `class_column`, `select`, `pixel_m` |

- Pixel areas are exact: on the WGS84 ellipsoid for maps in degrees, the map
  area divided by the CRS's area scale for projected maps.
- `aggregate: n` sums n x n source pixels into one (for example 10 m to
  100 m); `split: n` cuts each source pixel into n x n parts.
- Several tiles of one map (`files` with `*`) are read as one.
- Polygons are burned with every touched pixel counted (`all_touched`), on an
  equal-area grid of `pixel_m` metres, the share of each pixel counted on
  20 m sub-pixels.

### Alternatives

A map of the crop itself (a national field map, as the ATR/BPN rice fields for
Java) is the best crop mask. Without one:

| Dataset | Pixel | Crop | Setting | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [ESA WorldCover 2021 v200](https://esa-worldcover.org) | 10 m | cropland (class 40) | `values: classes`, `classes: [40]`, `aggregate: 10` | CC BY 4.0 |
| [GFSAD LGRIP30](https://doi.org/10.5067/Community/LGRIP/LGRIP30.001) | 30 m | irrigated (2) and rainfed (3) cropland, nominal 2015 | `classes: [2, 3]` | NASA LP DAAC, Earthdata login |
| [MapSPAM 2020 v2r2](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/SWPENT) | 5 arc-min (about 9 km) | physical area of 46 crops, by technology | `values: ha`, file `..._A_RICE_A.tif` for rice | CC BY 4.0 (IFPRI terms of the Dataverse record) |
| [C3S / ESA CCI land cover](https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.006f2c9a) | 300 m, yearly, 1992 to 2025 | rainfed cropland (10, 11, 12), irrigated or post-flooding cropland (20), cropland mosaic (30) | `values: classes`, `classes: [10, 11, 12, 20]` | ESA CCI licence (1992-2015), VITO licence or CC BY by version (Climate Data Store record) |
| [MODIS MCD12Q1 v061](https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/documents/1409/MCD12_User_Guide_V61.pdf) | 500 m | IGBP croplands (12), cropland mosaics (14) | `classes: [12, 14]` | NASA LP DAAC |

A general cropland class does not say which crop grows there: with it, the crop
of the experiment is simulated on all cropland. MapSPAM is crop-specific but
coarse, and its pixels place reported statistics with a model. The Java case
study compares all four with the national rice map:
[alternative inputs on Java](../java/alternatives.qmd).

### What the checks refuse

A raster without a CRS or not north-up; a mask that does not cover
`aoi > bbox`; `units_per_ha` of zero or less; a class band the file does not
have.

## Soil

**Used for:** the soil profile of every simulated season. Each weather cell
with crop gets one profile.

### Standard form

- A DSSAT `.SOL` file and `soil_map.csv`: one row per weather cell with crop,
  with the cell (`iy`, `ix`), its profile (`soil_id`), its crop area (`ha`) and
  the share of that area on the profile (`share`).
- At most 20 layers per profile, the engine's limit (`NL = 20` in
  `ModuleDefs.for`).
- A soil belongs to one weather grid and one crop mask: it has a profile only
  for the cells with crop. `input.json` records both, and the checks refuse the
  soil with another weather input or crop mask.
- Each cell gets its own copy of its profile (ID `XS<row><col>`), so settings
  per cell or stratum, such as the soil fertility factor `SLPF`, apply to that
  cell only.

### Bring your own

Section `prepare > soil`, then `python scripts/prepare_soils.py --aoi <aoi>`.

`method: sol` takes your own profiles from a `.SOL` file (a soil survey, WISE,
the generic HC27 profiles):

- `profile:` one profile for every cell, or
- `map:` which profile lies where: a raster of codes with `classes:` (a CSV of
  `code, soil_id`) or a vector file with `id_column:`. Each cell takes the
  profile under most of its crop; a cell whose crop lies wholly off the map
  takes the profile of the nearest cell that has one.

`method: soilgrids` builds a profile per cell from SoilGrids 2.0: the
crop-weighted mean of every property and depth under the cell's crop, turned
into DSSAT layers with the pedotransfer functions of Saxton and Rawls (2006)
([`src/soils.py`](https://github.com/bennyistanto/xdssat/blob/main/src/soils.py)).

- It reads a local copy of SoilGrids (`paths > soilgrids`, the layout of the
  ISRIC download site). `python scripts/fetch_soilgrids.py --aoi <aoi>`
  downloads the tiles an area lacks (`--dry-run` counts them);
  `python scripts/build_soilgrids_cache.py --aoi <aoi>` copies the area into one
  file per layer, which makes preparing faster.
- `soc_scale` scales SoilGrids organic carbon to measured profiles:
  `wise_indonesia`, `none`, or six factors by depth.
  `python scripts/fit_soc_scale.py --country <name>` fits the factors to the
  WISE profiles of a country and prints the setting.

| Country | 0-30 cm | 30-100 cm | 100-200 cm | WISE profiles |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Indonesia | 0.70 | 0.63 | 0.47 | 78 |
| Philippines | 0.72 | 0.83 | 0.64 | 49 |
| Thailand | 0.72 | 0.61 | 0.58 | 50 |
| India | 0.70 | 0.86 | 0.75 | 92 |

The factors are the median WISE / SoilGrids ratio of organic carbon per depth
band (WISE 1.1 in DSSAT's `WI.SOL`). The topsoil factor is close to 0.7 in all
four countries; the deeper ones differ, so factors fitted for one country do not
carry over to another.

### Alternatives

| Dataset | Content | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [SoilGrids 2.0](https://doi.org/10.5194/soil-7-217-2021) | 250 m, six depths to 200 cm: texture, organic carbon, bulk density, coarse fragments, nitrogen, pH, CEC | `method: soilgrids`; CC BY 4.0 |
| HC27 generic profiles | 27 profiles by texture, rooting depth and organic carbon (HarvestChoice), in DSSAT's `HC.SOL` | `method: sol` with one `profile:`; the file's header explains how to choose one |
| WISE 1.1 profiles | 3,404 measured profiles worldwide, in DSSAT's `WI.SOL` | `method: sol`, or to fit `soc_scale` |
| [HWSD v2.0](https://doi.org/10.4060/cc3823en) | about 1 km soil mapping units with seven depths to 200 cm (FAO and IIASA, 2023) | xdssat has no reader for it: turn its units into profiles of a `.SOL` file, then `method: sol` with `map:`; the FAO metadata states no licence, so check the terms of the download |

### What the checks refuse

A profile ID of the map that the file does not have; a profile with more than
20 layers; a soil made for another weather input or crop mask, or with other
sub-points of the crop mask.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Tested on Java

- One SoilGrids profile per BBSDLP soil-map class inside each cell, instead of
  one per cell (`scripts/soil_class_sensitivity.py`, 30 cells, 2015-2016):
  5.3 times the seasons; area-weighted yields changed by 0.0% (irrigated dry),
  -0.1% (irrigated wet) and -0.3% (rainfed); per cell the median change was
  0.0% and the largest 5.9%. SoilGrids varies smoothly, so this does not show
  how much a survey with its own profile per class would change; the script
  measures that for any class map.
- The organic carbon factors: `none` instead of `wise_indonesia` (30 cells,
  2015-2016) changed area-weighted yield by -0.2% (irrigated) and -2.5%
  (rainfed), and irrigation water by +10.5%.
- One profile for all of Java, the IRRI soil of the template (`IBRI910002`):
  rainfed yield 6,099 kg/ha against 8,003 kg/ha with SoilGrids (2015-2016).
- Central Luzon (Philippines): the SoilGrids copy had every tile; profiles for
  166 cells took 2.2 minutes from the tiles, or 14 s from an area cache built
  once in 2.3 minutes, with the same result.
:::

## Water regime

**Used for:** whether a crop pixel is managed as irrigated or rainfed. The
water regimes and their management levels in the template are set in
`treatments > water_regimes`; the seasons each regime is planted in, in
`seasons > calendar`.

### Standard form

One of:

- **A class map:** a GeoTIFF of codes and a class table (`code, name`).
  `treatments > water_regimes > <regime> > irrigation_classes` lists the codes
  of each regime.
- **An irrigated share:** a GeoTIFF of the irrigated share of each pixel (0-1,
  no value where unknown). Each crop pixel's area is split: the share goes to
  `treatments > share_regimes > share` (irrigated), the rest to `rest`
  (rainfed).

The map may be on any grid and CRS; it is read at the crop pixels.

**Optional.** `treatments > default_regime` gives a regime to crop the map does
not cover: crop on code 0, on a code no regime lists, or where the share has no
value, and all crop when there is no water regime input. With
`default_regime: null`, such crop stops the run with the area it concerns.

### Bring your own

Section `prepare > water_regime`, then `python scripts/prepare_layers.py`.

| `values:` | Map |
|---|---|
| `classes` | a raster of codes (with `classes:`, a CSV of `code, name`), several tiles (`files` with `*`), or a vector file with `class_column:` |
| `fraction`, `percent` | a raster of the irrigated share |
| `ratio` | two rasters of crop area on one grid, `irrigated:` and `total:` |

### Alternatives

A national irrigation map (as the Ministry of Agriculture map for Java) is the
best water regime. Without one:

| Dataset | Content | Setting | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| [GFSAD LGRIP30](https://doi.org/10.5067/Community/LGRIP/LGRIP30.001) | 30 m classes, nominal 2015: 0 water, 1 non-cropland, 2 irrigated, 3 rainfed; 10° x 10° tiles | `values: classes`, `files: "{inputs}/lgrip30/LGRIP30_2015_*.tif"`; irrigated `[2]`, rainfed `[3]`, `default_regime: rainfed` | overall 86.5% globally, 79.2% in Southeast Asia ([user guide](https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/documents/1619/LGRIP30_User_Guide_v1.pdf)) |
| [MapSPAM 2020 v2r2](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/SWPENT) | irrigated physical area of a crop over all its physical area, 5 arc-min | `values: ratio`, `irrigated: ..._A_RICE_I.tif`, `total: ..._A_RICE_A.tif` | not given per pixel |
| [FAO GMIA v5](https://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/geospatial-information/global-maps-irrigated-areas/latest-version) | area equipped for irrigation around 2005, in percent of each 5 arc-min cell, all crops [@siebert2013] | `values: percent` | not given per pixel; no licence stated on the download page |

LGRIP30 calls a cropland irrigated when it has "at least one artificial
irrigation during the crop growing period", and its cropland includes
plantations. Both maps are compared with the national map on Java in
[alternative inputs on Java](../java/alternatives.qmd).

### What the checks refuse

A class map without a class table; a share above 1 (or above 100 with
`percent`); a map that does not cover `aoi > bbox`.

## Region and zones

**Region** (optional): a class map; `aoi > region` names the class to keep, so
only crop inside it is simulated. Without a region input set
`aoi > region: null`, and `aoi > bbox` alone decides.

**Zones** (optional): a class map for `seasons > mode: by_zone`, one planting
calendar per zone: from `seasons > zone_table`, or the median rainfall onset of
each zone's cells.

Both: section `prepare > region` or `prepare > zones` with `values: classes`
(a raster with a class table, several tiles, or a vector file with
`class_column`), then `python scripts/prepare_layers.py`. A vector file is
burned on an equal-area grid of `pixel_m` metres (default 100), every touched
pixel counted. Administrative boundaries of the country, or an agro-ecological
zone map, are the usual sources.

## Planting dates

Planting dates are not an input kind: `seasons` sets them, as one calendar
(`mode: uniform`), one date per zone (`mode: by_zone` with a `zone_table`), or
from the rainfall onset of each weather cell (`mode: per_cell`). A gridded crop
calendar can set them by zone: classify its planting dates into a class map,
make it the `zones` input (`prepare_layers.py`), and give each class its date in
`seasons > zone_table`.

| Dataset | Content | Licence |
|---|---|---|
| [GGCMI phase 3 crop calendar](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5062513) | 0.5°, planting and maturity day of 18 crops, rainfed and irrigated, multi-year mean; two seasons for rice and wheat [@jagermeyr2021] | CC BY 4.0 (Zenodo record) |
| [MIRCA2000](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7422506) | 5 arc-min, monthly irrigated and rainfed growing area of 26 crops around 2000, with cropping calendars [@portmann2010] | CC BY 4.0 (Zenodo record) |
| [SAGE crop calendar](https://sage.nelson.wisc.edu/data-and-models/datasets/crop-calendar-dataset) | 5 arc-min and 0.5°, planting and harvest dates of 19 crops [@sacks2010] | no licence stated; the site asks users to tell the author of a download |

Licences above were read from each dataset's own record on 9 November 2026.
